vignette:
Marcus

Marcus is nineteen years old and works as a detective with the city police department—a position he secured through a youth recruitment program designed to bring younger officers into investigative roles. He carries himself with the careful precision of someone who has learned to control his environment, though his girlfriend notices he's become increasingly distant over the past eight months.

The captivity happened last winter, during what should have been a routine undercover operation. Marcus was embedded with a suspected trafficking ring, gathering intelligence for a larger investigation. What the department didn't anticipate was how quickly the situation would deteriorate. Within seventy-two hours, his cover was blown. He was locked in a basement with three other men—some of whom were victims themselves, their desperation palpable in the darkness. The captors were unpredictable. Sometimes they brought food; sometimes they didn't. Sometimes they asked questions; sometimes they simply stood in the doorway, watching. Marcus learned to read the footsteps on the stairs, to position himself in the corner where he could see the door, to make himself small and compliant. He was released after six days when a raid team located the property, but those six days have stretched across every day since.

Now, when Marcus sits at his desk reviewing case files, he finds himself unable to concentrate. His mind loops back to that basement—the smell of mold and human waste, the sound of chains, the particular quality of darkness that seemed to have weight. He'll be reading a witness statement, and suddenly his heart is racing, his palms are sweating, and he's convinced he's still down there. His colleagues have started to notice. He volunteers for fewer assignments. He's taken to keeping his office door open, unable to tolerate enclosed spaces. Last month, when an elevator malfunctioned with him inside for three minutes, he had what he describes as a "complete breakdown"—hyperventilating, convinced he couldn't get out, pounding on the doors until security released him.

At night, Marcus lies awake beside his girlfriend, listening to her breathe, waiting for the moment when sleep might come. When it does, he's back in that basement. He wakes gasping, sometimes shouting, and she's learned not to touch him during these episodes because his body doesn't recognize her in those first disorienting seconds. They've stopped being intimate. He can't tolerate being restrained, even gently, even in tenderness. She's tried to talk to him about it, but Marcus struggles to explain why the feeling of her weight against him, or her arms around him, triggers a suffocating panic that he can't control.

He's hypervigilant in ways he wasn't before. Driving to work, he maps exits. In restaurants, he positions himself to see all entrances. He's begun carrying his service weapon even off-duty, needing the weight of it against his ribs. When his captain suggested he take administrative leave, Marcus refused—the thought of sitting at home, alone with his thoughts, felt worse than pushing through. But pushing through is becoming harder. He's drinking more, staying up later, moving through his days in a kind of fog. He knows something is wrong. He knows the way he's living isn't sustainable. But asking for help feels like admitting that the captivity has won, that it's still holding him even though he's physically free.
